To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a class of postprocessing techniques for mixed finite element methods can be applied to meshes with triangular or tetrahedral elements and that these techniques recover second-order accurate velocities on certain special lines.
the postprocessors recover second-order accurate approximations of the solution of a second-order elliptic equation on triangular meshes.

the lowest-order mixed methods on triangles and tetrahedra yield first-order accurate velocity approximations, that a local postprocessor can be applied to these velocity approximations to yield a second-order accurate velocity field, and that this local postprocessing technique is a special case of a more general class of local postprocessors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Given the flux vector approximation from the hybrid mixed method on a triangular mesh, what is a good way to compute a second-order accurate velocity field?
the following question: Can a mixed finite element scheme for a second-order elliptic equation be modified to yield superconvergence in a certain sense?
the following questions: 1) Can a finite element velocity field on a triangular or tetrahedral mesh be used to compute second-order accurate flux vectors?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the flux vectors from lowest-order mixed methods on triangles are only first-order, but that the velocity fields are second-order accurate at special points, and that these special points include the vertices, edges, and faces of the elements.

the fluxes from the lowest-order hybrid mixed method on triangular and tetrahedron meshes are first-order accurate, but that the velocity fields are second-order accurate on three lines and on certain points on the mesh.

the flux vectors from the mixed finite element methods are first order accurate and the velocity vectors from the postprocessing technique are second-order accurate on triangular and tetrahedron meshes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the flux vectors from the hybrid mixed method are first-order accurate and can be postprocessed to recover second-order accuracy.
a postprocessing step can be applied to a mixed method to recover a second-order accurate velocity field from a first-order accurate mixed velocity and pressure approximation.
we can recover second order accurate fluxes from lowest order mixed finite element methods on triangular and tetrahedron meshes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for certain mixed methods, the fluxes from the lowest-order mixed method are not accurate but can be recovered to second-order accuracy by a local postprocessing step.
the superconvergence phenomenon is not limited to rectangular grids.
a simple local postprocessing technique can recover a second-order accurate velocity field from a first-order accurate flux vector.
